title: Who is worthier than you
hookLine: tradition says the nine-year-old told his father no one was worthier to answer the Kashmiris' plea
tomorrow: a court of poets at Anandpur

lines: A CHILD SAYS WHAT EVERYONE KNOWS.
cards: Anandpur, 1675, the scene from day seventy-seven. The pandits of Kashmir have told their story. The Guru sits in silence, heavy with it.

The boy from Patna, about nine now and living with his father at last, walks in, sees his father's face, and asks what's wrong. Sometimes a child says the thing the adults have been circling for hours.
The family is arguing about moving grandma in, and a seven-year-old says, well, she's lonely, isn't she? The room goes quiet. Everyone knew.

teach.b: Here is the exchange as Sikh tradition tells it. Guru Tegh Bahadur explains, simply, what the pandits have come for: they're being forced to give up their faith, and nobody can protect them.
Then he says the hard part out loud.

teach.h: IT WOULD TAKE A GREAT SACRIFICE.
teach.b: It would take the sacrifice of a great and holy person to stop this. The boy thinks about it, the way children do, completely seriously.
And he answers: who could be worthier than you, father?
A handful of words from a nine-year-old. Tradition is clear that the boy understood what he was saying. He was offering his father.
And his father heard it not as a child's mistake, but as an answer. Tradition says the Guru was glad, because he saw that his son was ready to lead.

He told the pandits to go to the authorities and say: if Guru Tegh Bahadur accepts conversion, we all will. Then he named Gobind Rai as the next Guru and set out for Delhi, knowing where the road went.

You already know the rest. What Sikhs take from this moment is the courage of the boy: a child of nine gave up his father for people who weren't even his community, because it was right. That boy became the tenth Guru.
The line people carry from it is simpler: when something needs doing, and you're wondering who should do it, sometimes the honest answer is: who better than you?

how: Sikhs often tell this story to children, and honor Guru Gobind Singh as the one who, at nine, encouraged his father to stand for the Kashmiri pandits.

games.q: you're nine. your father says it would take a great and holy person's sacrifice to save the pandits. what do you say?
o: who could be worthier than you?
games.why: tradition says Gobind Rai answered: who could be worthier than you? his father heard it as the answer, and named him Guru.

practice: Bring to mind someone at the edge of something hard: a surgery, a hard conversation, a new job, a decision they're afraid of. Picture their face, and picture yourself saying to them, simply and warmly: you can do this.

wordCard.voice: Gobind Rai. The tenth Guru's name as a boy, who at nine years old told his father there is no one worthier than you.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Gobind Rai, the tenth Guru's name before he became Gobind Singh.

carryVoice: Your line: who better than you. A few words from a child, and his father heard an answer. See you tomorrow.
